name: Red Fort: The Making of Shahjahanabad
description: More than a royal residence, the Red Fort was the heart of Shahjahanabad.This walk explores the Red Fort as a carefully designed imperial world where architecture, ceremony, water and power came together to express the grandeur of the Mughal Empire. Participants journey through its surviving palaces, audience halls and gardens to understand how the emperor's authority was physically staged and experienced within the fort. From the public spectacle of the Diwan-i-Aam to the private elegance of the imperial apartments, every space reveals a different aspect of Mughal courtly life.The experience also explores the transformation of the fort across centuries, from the glory of Shah Jahan's reign to the changing political fortunes of the Mughal Empire and the events that reshaped its identity in the colonial period. Through architecture and storytelling, the walk reveals the Red Fort not simply as a monument, but as the centre of an imperial vision that once shaped the life and identity of an entire city.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Shah Jahan's decision to establish Shahjahanabad and the role of the Red Fort as the political and ceremonial heart of the new Mughal capital.Enter the fort and examine its strategic location, monumental architecture and relationship with the wider city of Shahjahanabad.Explore the Diwan-i-Aam and understand the rituals of Mughal kingship, public audiences and the carefully designed relationship between the emperor and his subjects.Visit the Diwan-i-Khas and examine the world of imperial privilege, courtly culture and the political symbolism expressed through its extraordinary architecture.Trace the Nahr-i-Bihisht, or Stream of Paradise, and understand the importance of water in Mughal architecture, garden design and ideas of paradise.Explore the imperial residential spaces and discuss the daily life, privacy and ceremonial practices of the Mughal court.Examine the architectural language of the Red Fort and understand how materials, ornamentation, gardens and water were brought together to create an idealised imperial landscape.Discuss the changing fortunes of the Mughal Empire and the transformation of the fort as imperial power gradually declined.Conclude with the later history and legacy of the Red Fort, reflecting on how a seventeenth-century imperial palace became one of the most powerful symbols of Delhi and India's historical memory.Key Themes & Highlights Shah Jahan and the making of ShahjahanabadMughal imperial architectureArchitecture of powerRoyal court and ceremonyDiwan-i-Aam and Diwan-i-KhasImperial palaces and private lifeWater architecture and the Nahr-i-BihishtMughal gardens and aestheticsDecline of Mughal powerTransformation of the Red Fort through history

name: Possession: The Ghost, The Priest & The Asylum
description: About the LectureWe understand illness through a familiar triangle: the body, the mind, and society. Medicine, psychology, and social work divide it between themselves. But this framework, however useful, has always struggled to account for what happens when a community understands suffering not as malfunction, but as divine visitation — when ghosts replace hormones and deities replace doctors.This lecture moves through three distinct territories. First, the sociology of illness — how suffering is experienced, symbolised, and socially perceived. Then, the power embedded in medical knowledge itself, through Foucault and contemporary political discourse. And finally, into the Jagar ritual tradition, where spirit possession fractures the clean line between health and unhealth, and suffering becomes something altogether more complicated than a problem to be solved.This is not a lecture about superstition versus science. It is about whose knowledge counts, who gets to define suffering, and what gets lost when we insist on only one answer.The session explores:The sociology of illness: how suffering is experienced, symbolised, and socially perceivedThe power embedded in medical knowledge, through Foucault and contemporary political discourseThe Jagar ritual tradition and what spirit possession reveals about the limits of clinical frameworksWhose knowledge counts when two systems of understanding collideAbout the SpeakerShambhavi Tiwari is a doctoral research scholar at the Centre for Political Studies, JNU, and a Political Research Associate at Think Small, Connaught Place. She writes poetry and short fiction in Hindi, with publications in Hindwi and Sadaneera. She is motivated by her passion for ghosts, gods, dogs, cats, and a thorough hatred for anything premised on individualisation, obedience, or violence.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Heritage Walk : Shadows of Jahanpanah
description: Among Delhi's many historic cities, Jahanpanah remains perhaps the most elusive. Conceived in the fourteenth century as an ambitious attempt to unite earlier settlements within a single fortified capital, it was envisioned as a city without precedent. Today, however, its grand design survives only in fragments—hidden mosques, crumbling walls, forgotten reservoirs, and scattered monuments quietly woven into the modern city. Shadows of Jahanpanah seeks to reconnect these surviving pieces and reveal the extraordinary vision that once shaped this landscape.As participants move through its surviving monuments, the experience explores the political ambitions of the Delhi Sultanate, the ingenuity of medieval urban planning, and the architectural innovations that distinguished this remarkable capital. Beyond the monuments themselves lie larger questions about memory, impermanence, and the cities history chooses to celebrate or forget. Through historical interpretation, architectural observation, and compelling storytelling, the walk reconstructs a city that has almost vanished from sight, inviting participants to imagine the scale, complexity, and ambition of one of medieval India's most fascinating experiments in urban design.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Jahanpanah vision of Delhi's fourth city.Visit Satpula and examine medieval hydraulic engineering and defensive architecture.Explore Khirki Masjid while understanding the evolution of Sultanate mosque architecture.Visit Shaikh Yusuf Qattal's Tomb and discuss Sufi traditions during the Delhi Sultanate.Explore Begumpur Masjid, one of Delhi's grandest congregational mosques, and its urban significance.Conclude at Bijay Mandal while reconstructing the scale and ambition of Jahanpanah's royal citadel.Final discussion on medieval urban planning, the rise and decline of imperial cities, and the importance of preserving Delhi's lesser-known heritage.Key Themes & Highlights Tughlaq & Khilji dynastyMedieval urban planningSultanate architectureWater managementForgotten city of DelhiMonumental mosquesHidden heritage

name: The FishMarket #2
description: A FishMarket isn't a lecture. It's a room full of concerned citizens trying to solve a problem together.This one is about something we all experience every single day, and almost never stop to actually diagnose.Moving through a city should be simple. And yet an ordinary journey on foot, by bicycle, motorcycle or car routinely becomes an exercise in negotiation. The footpath disappears into parking. The pedestrian steps onto the road. The rider squeezes through a gap that probably shouldn't exist. The car stops wherever space appears. Each decision seems reasonable to the person making it. Together, they produce confusion, delay, and risk.But here's what we rarely ask: is this actually about bad civic sense? Or is it about a street that was designed without ever considering how people actually use it?This FishMarket will investigate how everyday disorder is created across the entire street. We'll will diagnose situations. We'll ask who or what shapes them. And then we'll move from diagnosis to solutions, examining which responsibilities belong to citizens, drivers, vendors, planners and authorities, and what changes in behaviour, rules, or design could actually help.Come ready to observe, challenge easy assumptions, and propose a better way for everyone to share the city.

description: Beneath Lodhi Garden's green landscape lies the memory of a turbulent period in the history of the Delhi Sultanate. Scattered across the gardens are magnificent tombs and monuments belonging to the Sayyid and Lodi periods, preserving a fascinating chapter of political transition, architectural experimentation and changing ideas of power.This walk explores Lodhi Gardens as more than a collection of beautiful monuments. Participants trace the evolution of tomb architecture from the Sayyid dynasty to the Lodi period, examining how changing political ambitions were expressed through domes, arches, ornamentation and carefully planned spaces. From the tomb of Muhammad Shah, with its distinctive octagonal form, to the enclosed garden tomb of Sikandar Lodi, the landscape reveals important developments in the history of Indo-Islamic architecture.The walk also explores monuments such as Bara Gumbad, Shish Gumbad and Athpula, uncovering their architectural significance and the stories surrounding them. Through tombs, gardens and forgotten structures, the experience reveals how Lodhi Gardens preserves the transition between the Delhi Sultanate and the world that would eventually give rise to Mughal Delhi.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Lodhi Gardens and the political landscape of fifteenth-century Delhi, when the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties ruled during the final centuries of the Delhi Sultanate.Visit Muhammad Shah's Tomb and examine its distinctive octagonal plan, architectural features and place within the evolution of Indo-Islamic funerary architecture.Explore the tomb of Sikandar Lodi and understand the changing relationship between tomb architecture, gardens and ideas of paradise. Discuss the reign of Sikandar Lodhi.Visit Bara Gumbad and examine its monumental architecture, discussing the purpose and architectural significance of the structure and its relationship with the adjoining mosque.Explore the mosque and surrounding structures, observing the development of arches, domes, decorative elements and spatial design during the Lodi period.Visit Shish Gumbad and discuss its distinctive ornamentation, architectural form and the continuing mystery surrounding the identities of those buried within.Walk through the wider landscape of Lodhi Gardens, understanding how these scattered monuments once existed within a historical landscape very different from the modern public garden seen today.Visit Athpula and explore its history and architectural significance, while discussing the importance of bridges, water and movement within Delhi's historic landscapes.Conclude with a discussion on the legacy of Sayyid and Lodi architecture and how the experiments of the Delhi Sultanate helped create architectural traditions that would later be transformed under the Mughals.

name: Purana Qila Heritage Walk
description: Purana Qila is more than the remains of a medieval capital, it is a landscape where mythology, archaeology and imperial ambition overlap. Often associated with the legendary city of Indraprastha, the site preserves layers of settlement and memory that make it one of the most fascinating places from which to explore Delhi's long history.This walk journeys through the many worlds contained within Purana Qila. Participants explore the debate surrounding Indraprastha and examine how archaeology helps us understand the deeper history buried beneath the visible fortifications. The experience then traces the rivalry between Humayun and Sher Shah Suri, whose competing visions transformed the site into successive imperial capitals - Dinpanah and Shergarh.From the monumental gateways and Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque to Sher Mandal and the excavation sites, each stop reveals a different layer of political ambition, architectural innovation and historical memory. Through stories of empire, exile, return and unfinished legacies, the walk explores how Delhi's cities were repeatedly built, destroyed, transformed and rebuilt upon the landscapes of those that came before.Detailed Flow of Walk	Introduction to Purana Qila as a landscape of multiple historical layers from Indraprastha to Partition.Enter through the monumental gateways and examine how fortifications, architecture and strategic planning reflected the ambitions of successive rulers.Explore the debate surrounding Indraprastha, discussing the relationship between mythology, historical memory and archaeological evidence.Visit the excavation sites and understand how archaeological layers help reconstruct the history of settlement at Purana Qila across different periods.Trace Humayun's vision of Dinpanah and discuss his attempt to establish a new imperial capital within this historic landscape.Explore the rivalry between Humayun and Sher Shah Suri and understand how Sher Shah transformed the site into Shergarh after taking control of the empire.Visit Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque and examine its architectural design, decorative details and significance as one of the important surviving examples of the period.Explore Sher Mandal and discuss its changing interpretations, its association with Humayun and the tragic story of the emperor's fall.Discover lesser-known structures and hidden corners within the fort, including its relationship with water, movement and the wider historical landscape.Conclude with stories of empire, exile, return and unfinished legacies, reflecting on how Delhi has repeatedly built new cities upon the memories and remains of older ones.

name: The Comfort of Illusions
description: About the LectureDo you think we're confusing the satisfaction of seeing someone punished with the achievement of preventing harm?Imagine that tomorrow we double prison sentences, lock up twice as many people, and criminalise ten new things. The public cheers, the politicians declare victory, and the law looks tougher than it has ever looked. But the violence continues, the vulnerable stay vulnerable, and the conditions that produce harm go untouched. We would have punished more people more harshly. Would we have made anyone safer?We have a deep faith in punishment: that crime makes us unsafe, that criminals are the problem, and that harsher laws and longer sentences are the price of a safer society. Punishment reassures us that the bad have been identified, the dangerous contained, and the rest of us protected.Anup Surendranath has spent his career inside that system. He and his team have represented nearly 200 death-row prisoners and thousands of undertrials. This lecture turns the question back on us: if we truly understood how criminal justice works, would we still believe what we believe about punishment — and would we care enough to change it?The session explores:Why punishment feels like safety, and why the two are not the same thingWhat the criminal justice system actually does to the people who pass through itWhy obsessing over the rotten fruit means never examining the tree that keeps producing itWhat it would really take to build a society in which fewer people are harmedAbout the SpeakerAnup Surendranath is Professor of Law and Executive Director of The Square Circle Clinic (formerly Project 39A) at NALSAR University of Law. He studied law at NALSAR Hyderabad and completed his master's and doctorate at the University of Oxford before returning to teach at India's leading law schools and work on the ground with the criminal justice system. At The Square Circle Clinic, he and his team have represented nearly 200 death-row prisoners and thousands of undertrials. As an adolescent, he was convinced that justice sometimes required a good cop to burn the bad guy alive — a certainty he credits the 1994 Malayalam blockbuster Commissioner, and several summers of rented video cassettes, with instilling. Life, and a rather good education, complicated it.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Who Does the City Belong To?
description: Who Does the City Belong To?A conversation on public space and the lawYou have probably stood in front of a barricade this year. A road closed with no notice. A park gate locked at night. A station shut, a lane that used to be a shortcut now ending in a guard and a boom. Most of us have learned to route around it without thinking.But there’s a question underneath that almost none of us can answer: what are we actually entitled to in a public space and what happens when that space is closed, fenced or policed?In the first edition of The Human City Conversations, the urbanist Jagan Shah described a Delhi increasingly run by barricades and closures, and someone in the audience said that what privilege buys in this city is isolation. This conversation picks up exactly where that one stopped, because the next question is a legal one.We’ll ask what the Constitution actually gives us by way of a right to assemble and to protest. Whether a government can simply take a Jantar Mantar away. Whether there is such a thing as a right to walk in an Indian city, and who in Delhi really has it. And how much of what we call planning is in truth a question of who is expected to justify their presence in public, and who is not.It isn’t a lecture, and it isn’t a complaint session. It’s an hour of conversation, in plain words, followed by your questions put directly to someone who has spent two decades arguing these things in court.About the guestMihira Sood is a lawyer and scholar in the field of women’s rights, and practices at the Supreme Court of India and the Delhi High Court. She has taught at Jindal Global Law School and National Law University Delhi, and holds degrees from NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and Columbia Law School, New York. She was among the youngest members to assist the Justice Verma Committee, whose recommendations reshaped India’s criminal law on sexual violence. She writes and speaks widely on women’s rights, feminist jurisprudence, equality law and civil liberties, and is a regular commentator in the national press. She has recently written a book Courting Equality which focusses on the Landmark Cases in the Battle for Women’s Rights (Juggernaut) traces fifty years of the law’s encounter with women’s lives — from the anti-dowry agitations of the 1970s, through Shah Bano and the Uniform Civil Code debate, to the Nirbhaya movement and its continuing reverberations, and on to the present backlash against the supposed misuse of these very laws.Copies will be on sale at Kunzum on the evening, at 20% off.About the seriesThe Human City Conversations is the live edition of The Human City Podcast, hosted by Ruchita Bansal, which for the past year has asked how Indian cities are planned, built and experienced — and who they are built for. The podcast’s questions, taken off the feed and into a room, in public, in Delhi.The detailsSunday 1 November 2026, 5 PM onwardsKunzum Books, GK-2, New DelhiLimited seats · Tickets on Urbanaut

name: Sacred Streets of Shahjahanabad
description: Beyond the crowded bazaars and familiar landmarks of Old Delhi lies a carefully layered historic city shaped by faith, community, poetry and a distinctive way of urban life. Participants explore the differences between a kucha, katra and gali, discovering how these distinct urban spaces shaped community life and movement through the city. The walk also examines the design of traditional havelis and the architectural principles that created private worlds behind their seemingly modest street-facing entrances.From the remarkable legacy of Digambar Jain Lal Mandir and Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib to the hidden heritage of Naughara and the enduring presence of Fatehpuri Masjid, the walk reveals how different communities shaped the city. A visit to Ghalib ki Haveli adds another layer, connecting Shahjahanabad's streets with the literary and cultural world of nineteenth-century Delhi.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Shahjahanabad as a planned Mughal city and an exploration of how its streets, markets and neighbourhoods developed around communities, occupations, faith and everyday life.Visit Digambar Jain Lal Mandir and explore the remarkable legacy of Delhi's oldest Jain temple while understanding the relationship between sacred spaces and the surrounding urban neighbourhood.Continue to Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib and uncover its powerful story of faith, sacrifice and resilience within the historic landscape of Chandni Chowk.Walk through the historic streets and neighbourhoods of Shahjahanabad while understanding the difference between a kucha, katra and gali, and how these spaces shaped movement, trade, privacy and community life.Explore Naughara and discover its hidden Jain temples and beautifully preserved heritage havelis.Understand how traditional havelis were designed, from their relationship with the street to the organisation of private and shared spaces within, and examine how architecture responded to the social life of the city.Continue through the hidden streets of Chandni Chowk, discovering architectural details and neighbourhood stories that reveal how Shahjahanabad functioned as a living city.Visit Ghalib ki Haveli and step into the literary world of Mirza Ghalib, exploring poetry, culture and everyday life in nineteenth-century Delhi.Visit Fatehpuri Masjid and understand its significance within the urban and commercial landscape of Shahjahanabad.Conclude with a discussion on how faith, communities, neighbourhood planning and architecture came together to create one of India's most remarkable living historic cities.

description: An OutClass Bar Lecture with Gaurav GillABOUT THE SESSION Every conversation has a second layer. Learn to notice it.Someone says they’re fine, but something feels off. A job candidate sounds confident, but their delivery tells a different story. A first date is going well — or is it? And what can a handshake, a fleeting expression or a change in posture actually tell you?We communicate even when we aren’t speaking. But how much can you really tell from the way someone looks, moves, listens and responds?Join Gaurav Gill, Consultant Psychologist and Body Language Expert, for an eye-opening evening that takes you inside the fascinating world of non-verbal communication. Drawing on real-world investigative experience, forensic psychology and high-stakes interactions, Gaurav will show you how to observe human behaviour with a sharper, more informed eye.What makes this especially interesting? The same principles of behavioural observation used in criminal investigations can also help us better understand everyday interactions — from first dates and friendships to job interviews, negotiations and workplace dynamics.WHO IS THIS FOR?The curious. The observant. The people who love figuring out what makes others tick.Whether you’re navigating dating, building your career, negotiating at work, studying psychology, or simply fascinated by human behaviour, this session will give you a fresh perspective on the conversations happening around you.No prior knowledge of psychology is needed. ABOUT THE SPEAKERFeatured on many podcasts, including Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast, in an episode that has drawn more than 3.2 million views. Gaurav has trained law enforcement personnel and forensic professionals across India, including Delhi Police Crime Branch AHTU, CISF, RPF and GRP, and has delivered expert sessions at institutions including the National Forensic Sciences University and Rashtriya Raksha University. He was also featured on WION analysing world leaders’ non-verbal cues around the 2026 BRICS Summit.Now, he brings these insights out of the classroom and into the bar.WHAT YOU’LL DISCOVER• The face behind the words: Understand facial expressions, gestures, posture and eye movements — and what they may reveal about a person’s emotional state.• Nervousness or something else? Explore the difference between ordinary stress, discomfort and behavioural changes that deserve a closer look.• Can you spot a lie? Challenge popular myths about deception and discover why no single gesture can reliably tell you whether someone is lying.• Read the room: Recognise shifts in engagement, comfort and interaction during conversations, meetings and social situations.• Make a stronger impression: Learn how your own body language can influence how you come across in interviews, presentations, negotiations and everyday encounters.THE OUTCLASS EXPERIENCEWe believe the best conversations don’t always happen in classrooms.The OutClass brings powerful ideas and fascinating people into bars and cafés, creating a space where you can enjoy a drink, discover something unexpected and leave with more to think about — and talk about.Come for the drink. Stay for the thought.One evening. A new lens on human behaviour. And conversations that might never look the same again.

We explore the stories, beliefs and rituals that have shaped the sacred imagination around this river for centuries.And as the evening gathers, we end where the river meets ritual.
